note: Hand-written Language Usage starter items (docs/03 §6): every item states its rule and CCSS code. Priority-1 skills first (LU.G.3, LU.G.4, LU.G.6, LU.M.6, LU.S.1), then October skills (LU.G.1, LU.G.2, LU.M.1, LU.M.2). The LLM bank refill adds more once the API key exists.

items.stem: Choose the verb that shows the action happened yesterday: Yesterday Aysel ___ her bike to school.
options: rides
rode
will ride
riding
items.explanation: "Yesterday" tells us the action is in the past, so we need the past tense: rode.
items.rule: L.5.1c — use verb tense to convey time.

items.stem: Which sentence is about the future?
options: Rasim plays football on Fridays.
Rasim played football last week.
Rasim will play football tomorrow.
Rasim is playing football now.
items.explanation: "Will play" and "tomorrow" both point to the future.

items.stem: Write the past tense of the verb in brackets: Last night we (eat) ___ dinner at my grandmother's house.
items.explanation: Eat is irregular: eat → ate.

items.stem: Which sentence shows that one action happened BEFORE another in the past?
options: By the time the bell rang, Leyla had finished her test.
Leyla finishes her test and the bell rings.
Leyla will finish her test before the bell rings.
Leyla is finishing her test as the bell rings.
items.explanation: "Had finished" (past perfect) shows the finishing happened before the ringing.

items.stem: Complete with the correct form of "go": Every summer my cousins ___ to Sheki, and they ___ there again next year.
items.explanation: A habit uses the simple present (go); "next year" needs the future (will go).
items.rule: L.5.1c — tense to convey time and state.

items.stem: Which sentence describes a condition (something that would happen only if something else happened)?
options: If it rains, we will stay inside.
It rained, so we stayed inside.
It is raining and we are inside.
It rains a lot in March.
items.explanation: "If … will" expresses a condition.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that the first action clearly happened before the second: "Kamran ate breakfast and left for school."
items.rubric: Accept any correct use of the past perfect for the first action, e.g. "Kamran had eaten breakfast before he left for school" or "After Kamran had eaten breakfast, he left for school." Must use had + past participle for eating.
items.explanation: Past perfect (had eaten) shows the earlier of two past actions.
items.rule: L.5.1c — sequence with the past perfect.

items.stem: Read: "By next June, Nigar ___ the piano for five years." Which verb form is correct?
options: will have played
played
has played
is playing

distractor_rationale.C: up to now, not up to a future point

items.explanation: The future perfect (will have played) shows an action completed by a future time.

items.stem: Explain the difference in meaning between "I have lived in Baku for ten years" and "I lived in Baku for ten years."
items.rubric: Must say that the first (present perfect) means the speaker still lives in Baku, while the second (simple past) means the speaker no longer lives there. Any wording that captures 'still true now' vs 'finished' is correct.
items.explanation: Present perfect connects the past to now; simple past is finished.

items.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in verb tense?
options: She opened the door and walked in.
She opened the door and walks in.
She opens the door and walks in.
She will open the door and walk in.
items.explanation: "Opened" is past but "walks" is present: an inappropriate shift.
items.rule: L.5.1d — avoid inappropriate shifts in verb tense.

items.stem: Fix the shift by changing the second verb: "The dog barked and then it runs away." Write the corrected second verb.
items.explanation: Barked is past, so runs must become ran.

items.stem: Choose the sentence with consistent verb tense.
options: Every morning I wake up, brushed my teeth and eat breakfast.
Every morning I wake up, brush my teeth and eat breakfast.
Every morning I woke up, brush my teeth and eat breakfast.
Every morning I wake up, brush my teeth and ate breakfast.
items.explanation: A habit stays in the present: wake, brush, eat.

items.stem: Read: "When the teacher entered, everyone stands up and greets her." Which words need to change to fix the tense shift?
options: entered
stands and greets
everyone
teacher

distractor_rationale.A: entered sets the past; keep it

items.explanation: Change stands → stood and greets → greeted to match "entered".

items.stem: Rewrite the sentence so the tense is consistent: "Murad picks up the ball, ran to the goal and scores."
items.rubric: Accept all-past ("Murad picked up the ball, ran to the goal and scored") or all-present ("Murad picks up the ball, runs to the goal and scores"). All three verbs must be in the same tense.
items.explanation: All three verbs must match: picked/ran/scored or picks/runs/scores.

items.stem: Which change is ALLOWED, because the time really does change?
options: "Yesterday I lost my key, but I will look for it tomorrow."
"Yesterday I lose my key, but I looked for it."
"I am looking for my key and found it yesterday."
"I will lose my key and looked for it."
items.explanation: A tense change is correct when the time changes (yesterday → tomorrow).

items.stem: This paragraph has two tense mistakes. Find both and write the corrected verbs: "Last Saturday we visit the museum. The guide showed us a golden helmet, and everyone gasps. Then we ate lunch in the garden."
items.rubric: Must identify: visit → visited, gasps → gasped. Both required for full credit; one for partial.
items.explanation: The paragraph is set last Saturday, so every verb should be past.
items.rule: L.5.1d — recognise and correct shifts in a paragraph.

items.stem: In a story written in the past tense, which sentence is correctly written?
options: The wind howled, and the shutters bang against the wall.
The wind howls, and the shutters banged against the wall.
The wind howled, and the shutters banged against the wall.
The wind will howl, and the shutters banged against the wall.
items.explanation: Both verbs stay in the past: howled, banged.

items.stem: Explain why this sentence is wrong and fix it: "She said she will come, but she never came."
items.rubric: Must note that "said" is past, so the reported future should be "would come" (past form), giving "She said she would come, but she never came."
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb, will becomes would.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb: The cats ___ sleeping on the sofa.
options: is
are
am
be
items.explanation: "Cats" is plural, so the verb is are.

items.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
options: Running down the hill.
The boy with the red hat.
The boy ran down the hill.
Because it was late.

distractor_rationale.D: a dependent clause on its own

items.explanation: A sentence needs a subject (the boy) and a verb (ran) and must make sense alone.

items.stem: Choose the pronoun: Leyla lost ___ umbrella on the bus.
items.explanation: Leyla is one girl, so the pronoun is her.

items.stem: Which sentence is a run-on?
options: I finished my homework, then I went outside.
I finished my homework, and then I went outside.
After I finished my homework, I went outside.
I finished my homework. Then I went outside.
items.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma make a run-on (comma splice).

items.stem: Choose the correct verb: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready for the fire drill.
options: was
were
is
be
items.explanation: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: students → were.

items.stem: Fix the pronoun: "Each of the boys brought their own lunch." Write the correct pronoun.
items.explanation: "Each" is singular, so the pronoun is singular: his.
items.rule: L.4.1 (review) — pronoun agrees with a singular antecedent.

items.stem: Rewrite this run-on as correct sentences: "The match started late it was raining the players were cold."
items.rubric: Accept any correct split, e.g. "The match started late because it was raining, and the players were cold." or three sentences. Must not leave two independent clauses joined without punctuation or a conjunction.
items.explanation: Separate the three ideas with full stops or joining words.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: The team are practising their new song.
The team is practising its new song.
The team is practising their new song.
The team are practising its new song.

distractor_rationale.A: team is singular in standard American usage

items.explanation: "Team" is a singular collective noun: is … its.

items.stem: Explain what is wrong with this sentence and fix it: "Rasim told Kamran that he had won the prize."
items.rubric: Must say the pronoun "he" is unclear (could be Rasim or Kamran) and rewrite to make the meaning clear, e.g. "Rasim told Kamran, 'You have won the prize.'" or "Rasim told Kamran that Kamran had won the prize."
items.explanation: A pronoun must clearly refer to one antecedent.

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalised correctly?
options: my friend sabina lives in baku.
My friend Sabina lives in Baku.
My Friend Sabina Lives In Baku.
My friend sabina lives in Baku.
items.explanation: Capitalise the first word, names of people and places.

items.stem: Which sentence punctuates the dialogue correctly?
options: "Let's go," said Murad.
"Let's go" said Murad.
"Let's go, said Murad."
Let's go, "said Murad."

distractor_rationale.C: closing quotation mark in the wrong place
distractor_rationale.D: quotation marks around the wrong words

items.explanation: Put the spoken words in quotation marks, with a comma before the closing mark.

items.stem: Write the two words that need a capital letter: "on monday we visited the caspian sea." (Write them separated by a comma, not counting the first word.)
items.explanation: Days of the week and place names take capitals.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Aysel asked, "can we go to the park?"
Aysel asked, "Can we go to the park?"
Aysel asked "Can we go to the park"?
Aysel asked, Can we go to the park?

distractor_rationale.A: the quotation must start with a capital
distractor_rationale.C: missing comma; question mark belongs inside

items.explanation: Comma after asked, capital letter to start the quotation, question mark inside the marks.

items.stem: Add the punctuation and capital letters: the coach shouted keep running elchin
items.rubric: Accept: The coach shouted, "Keep running, Elchin!" (also acceptable with a full stop instead of an exclamation mark). Must have: capital T, comma after shouted, quotation marks, capital K, capital E, end punctuation inside the marks.
items.explanation: Speaker tag, comma, quotation marks around the words spoken, capital at the start of the quotation.

items.stem: Which sentence uses capitals correctly?
options: We read a Book about Ancient Egypt in january.
We read a book about ancient Egypt in January.
We read a book about Ancient egypt in january.
we read a book about ancient egypt in January.

distractor_rationale.A: book and ancient are common words; January needs a capital
distractor_rationale.C: Egypt needs a capital; January too
distractor_rationale.D: first word and Egypt need capitals

items.explanation: Capitalise the first word, place names and months; not ordinary nouns.

items.stem: Write this as two lines of dialogue between Leyla and her father, with correct punctuation: Leyla says she finished her homework; her father asks whether she checked it.
items.rubric: Accept e.g.: "I finished my homework," said Leyla. "Did you check it?" asked her father. Must show: quotation marks around each speech, comma or question mark inside the closing marks, capital letters at the start of each quotation, speaker tags. Each speaker on a new line is a bonus, not required.
items.explanation: Each speaker's words go inside their own quotation marks, with a speaker tag.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly when the speaker tag comes in the middle?
options: "If we leave now," said Nigar, "we will catch the bus."
"If we leave now" said Nigar "we will catch the bus."
"If we leave now," said Nigar. "We will catch the bus."
"If we leave now, said Nigar, we will catch the bus."

distractor_rationale.C: a full stop splits one sentence
distractor_rationale.D: the tag must be outside the marks

items.explanation: A tag in the middle of one sentence is set off with commas, and the second part starts with a small letter.

items.stem: Find the three capitalisation mistakes and write the corrected words: "my Aunt lives near the mountains in Sheki, and Every summer we visit her in july."
items.rubric: Must give: My (first word), aunt (lower case: common noun), every (lower case), July (capital). Three or four corrections: my→My, Aunt→aunt, Every→every, july→July. Full credit for three correct.
items.explanation: Capitalise the first word and months; not ordinary nouns like aunt or words in the middle.

items.stem: Which sentence combines these two correctly? "The dog was hungry. The dog ate quickly."
options: The dog was hungry, so it ate quickly.
The dog was hungry it ate quickly.
The dog was hungry, ate quickly.
Hungry the dog quickly.
items.explanation: Join with a comma and a connecting word such as so.

items.stem: Which sentence adds a detail to "The bird sang"?
options: The bird sang.
The small bird sang sweetly from the fig tree.
Sang the bird.
Bird sang bird.
items.explanation: Adding adjectives and phrases expands a sentence.

items.stem: Combine into one sentence: "Nigar likes chess. Nigar likes swimming."
items.rubric: Accept: "Nigar likes chess and swimming." or "Nigar likes both chess and swimming." One sentence with 'and'.
items.explanation: Join the two objects with and.

items.stem: Reduce this sentence so it says the same thing in fewer words: "At this point in time, the students who are in my class are of the opinion that the test was really very hard."
items.rubric: Accept any clear shorter version keeping the meaning, e.g. "My classmates think the test was very hard." or "Now my classmates think the test was hard." Must remove wordy phrases like 'at this point in time', 'are of the opinion'.
items.explanation: Cut wordy phrases; keep the meaning.

items.stem: Which combined sentence keeps the meaning of "The rain stopped. We went outside. We played football." and sounds best?
options: When the rain stopped, we went outside and played football.
The rain stopped and we went outside and we played football and.
We played football, the rain stopped, we went outside.
The rain stopped we went outside we played football.
items.explanation: A time clause (when …) links the events smoothly.
items.rule: L.5.3a — combine for meaning and style.

items.stem: Expand this sentence with a detail that tells WHERE and one that tells WHEN: "The children played."
items.rubric: Accept any grammatical sentence adding a place and a time, e.g. "After school, the children played in the courtyard." Both a where-phrase and a when-phrase required.
items.explanation: Phrases like 'after school' and 'in the courtyard' add when and where.

items.stem: Rewrite the two sentences as ONE sentence that shows the reason: "Kamran was late. His bus broke down."
items.rubric: Accept: "Kamran was late because his bus broke down." or "Because his bus broke down, Kamran was late." Must use a reason word (because/since/as).
items.explanation: Because links the effect to its cause.

items.stem: A writer wants the sentence to sound more exciting. Which version is best?
options: The horse went over the fence.
The horse cleared the fence in one great leap and thundered across the field.
The horse went over the fence and then it went across the field.
Over the fence the horse went.
items.explanation: Strong verbs and a vivid phrase make the sentence lively.
items.rule: L.5.3a — expand for interest and style.

items.stem: Here are four short, choppy sentences. Rewrite them as two well-built sentences: "Sabina opened the box. It was empty. She was surprised. She had expected a gift."
items.rubric: Accept any two sentences that combine the ideas naturally, e.g. "When Sabina opened the box, she was surprised to find it empty. She had expected a gift." Must be exactly two sentences, grammatical, meaning kept.
items.explanation: Combining choppy sentences improves flow.
items.rule: L.5.3a — combine and reduce for style.

items.stem: Which word is a preposition in this sentence? "The cat hid under the table."
options: cat
hid
under
table
items.explanation: Under shows the position of the cat in relation to the table.

items.stem: Which word is an interjection?
options: quickly
Wow
because
table
items.explanation: Wow expresses a sudden feeling.

items.stem: What does the conjunction do in this sentence? "I wanted to swim, but the water was too cold."
options: It joins two ideas and shows a contrast.
It shows where something is.
It expresses a strong feeling.
It describes the water.
items.explanation: But joins two clauses and signals contrast.

items.stem: Choose the best conjunction: "You can have tea ___ juice, but not both."
items.explanation: Or offers a choice between two things.

items.stem: Write one sentence that contains a preposition, a conjunction AND an interjection. Then label each one.
items.rubric: Accept any grammatical sentence with all three correctly labelled, e.g. "Wow, the kite flew over the roof and landed in the garden!" — Wow (interjection), over/in (preposition), and (conjunction).
items.explanation: Interjection = feeling word; preposition = relationship of place/time; conjunction = joining word.
items.rule: L.5.1a — functions of the three parts of speech.

items.stem: In which sentence does "before" work as a conjunction (joining two clauses) rather than a preposition?
options: We ate before the film.
We ate before the film started.
Before dinner, we played.
He stood before the judge.
items.explanation: A conjunction is followed by a clause with its own verb: the film started.
items.rule: L.5.1a — the same word can be a preposition or a conjunction.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect tense?
options: I walk to school.
I walked to school.
I have walked to school every day this week.
I will walk to school.
items.explanation: Have + past participle (walked) forms the present perfect.

items.stem: Complete with the present perfect of "finish": She ___ ___ her project already.
items.explanation: She + has + past participle.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the past perfect correctly?
options: When we arrived, the film has started.
When we arrived, the film had started.
When we arrived, the film will have started.
When we arrived, the film starts.

distractor_rationale.A: present perfect does not fit a past arrival

items.explanation: Had started happened before we arrived.

items.stem: Complete with the future perfect of "leave": By the time you read this, I ___ ___ ___.
items.explanation: Will + have + past participle.

items.stem: Write three sentences about a football match: one in the present perfect, one in the past perfect, one in the future perfect. Label each.
items.rubric: Three grammatical sentences, each correctly labelled: present perfect (has/have + past participle), past perfect (had + past participle), future perfect (will have + past participle). Full credit needs all three correct forms.
items.explanation: Perfect tenses use a form of have with the past participle.
items.rule: L.5.1b — form and use perfect tenses.

items.stem: Why is the past perfect used here? "Aysel had already eaten when her friends arrived with pizza."
options: To show that eating happened before the friends arrived.
To show that eating will happen tomorrow.
To show that eating is happening now.
To show that the friends ate first.
items.explanation: Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events.
items.rule: L.5.1b — meaning of the past perfect.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly for a list?
options: We bought apples pears and grapes.
We bought apples, pears, and grapes.
We bought, apples, pears and grapes.
We bought apples, pears and, grapes.
items.explanation: Commas separate items in a series.

items.stem: Add the commas: "My favourite subjects are maths science and art."
items.rubric: Accept: My favourite subjects are maths, science, and art. (comma before 'and' optional). Commas after maths and science required.
items.explanation: Separate each item with a comma.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Rasim packed his boots, his gloves, and his hat.
Rasim packed his boots his gloves and his hat.
Rasim, packed his boots, his gloves and his hat.
Rasim packed, his boots, his gloves, and his hat.
items.explanation: Commas go between the items, not after the verb.

items.stem: Write a sentence listing four things you would take on a picnic, with correct commas.
items.rubric: Any grammatical sentence with four items separated by commas (comma before the final 'and' optional), e.g. "I would take sandwiches, juice, a blanket and a ball."
items.explanation: Commas separate the items in the series.
items.rule: L.5.2a — use series commas in writing.

items.stem: Which sentence needs commas because it lists three ACTIONS?
options: Leyla opened the window looked outside and smiled.
Leyla opened the window and smiled.
Leyla smiled at the window.
Leyla opened the big wooden window.

distractor_rationale.B: only two actions, no commas needed
distractor_rationale.D: adjectives, not a list of actions

items.explanation: Three actions in a row form a series: opened the window, looked outside, and smiled.

items.stem: Explain why the meaning changes with the comma: "I invited my parents, Aysel and Kamran." versus "I invited my parents, Aysel, and Kamran."
items.rubric: Must explain: without the final comma, 'Aysel and Kamran' can be read as naming the parents (two people invited); with the comma, four people are invited (parents plus Aysel plus Kamran). Any clear explanation of the ambiguity earns credit.
items.explanation: The final (Oxford) comma can prevent a misreading.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the comma after the introductory word correctly?
options: Yes, I will come to the party.
Yes I will, come to the party.
Yes I will come, to the party.
Yes I will come to the party,
items.explanation: A comma follows an introductory word like Yes.
items.rule: L.5.2b — comma after an introductory element.

items.stem: Add the comma: "After lunch we walked along the Boulevard."
items.rubric: Accept: After lunch, we walked along the Boulevard.
items.explanation: A comma follows the introductory phrase.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: When the bell rang, the students lined up.
When the bell rang the students, lined up.
When, the bell rang the students lined up.
When the bell rang the students lined up,
items.explanation: An introductory clause is followed by a comma.

items.stem: Write a sentence that begins with "Although" and uses the comma correctly.
items.rubric: Any grammatical sentence beginning with an 'Although …' clause followed by a comma and a main clause, e.g. "Although it was raining, we played outside."
items.explanation: The introductory clause ends with a comma.

items.stem: In which sentence is the comma NOT needed?
options: Finally, we reached the summit.
In the morning, the sea was calm.
We reached the summit, finally.
Because it was late, we hurried.
items.explanation: The comma rule is for elements at the START of a sentence; 'finally' at the end needs no comma.
items.rule: L.5.2b — where the introductory comma applies.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so it starts with the introductory phrase, and punctuate it: "We saw dolphins near the shore early in the morning."
items.rubric: Accept: "Early in the morning, we saw dolphins near the shore." Must move the phrase to the front and add the comma.
items.explanation: Moving the phrase to the front requires a comma after it.
